newsitem.title: GERMANY: Juan Carlos hits out at ETA on German visit.
newsitem.headline: Juan Carlos hits out at ETA on German visit.

text.p: King Juan Carlos of Spain on Wednesday condemned the murder of a 29-year-old town councillor by the Basque separatist group ETA, branding the guerrillas contemptible terrorists.

On the first full day of a visit to Germany, the king told a reception in Berlin city hall that the murder of the politician, Miguel Angel Blanco, was "as contemptible as the terrorists who killed him".
"We Spaniards are all in shock and I feel I must express my admiration for Miguel Angel as a person and for his life," said the king, who normally steers clear of political issues.

The king's language was stronger than comments he made in a televised address after Blanco's funeral on Monday. He said then that Blanco's death had not been in vain and praised the widespread revulsion to the killing.
Blanco, a member of Spain's ruling party, was kidnapped last Thursday by ETA rebels who vowed to kill him in 48 hours unless the government gave in to their demands.
They shot him twice in the head on Saturday and he died 12 hours later. The killing of an ordinary, low-ranking official stunned Spaniards.

At a reception at the Reichstag building, home of Germany's past and future parliament, the king did not refer directly to the killing but his message was clear as he handed over copies of the Spanish constitution from 1812 and 1978.
"The Spanish people gives the German people its word," he said. "And these words stand for the unswerving desire to live in freedom and peace. These words can be neither burned nor destroyed."
German President Roman Herzog said the spontaneous reaction of the Basque people who took to the streets in massive numbers to protest against the murder was a positive sign.
"This makes me, in all sadness and horror at the senseless death of a human being, hopeful about the future," Herzog said according to the text of his speech at an evening banquet.

Berlin mayor Eberhard Diepgen thanked the king for going ahead with his visit, his first to Berlin since 1986. "In the name of all Berliners, allow me to express our sympathies and concern in this difficult situation," he said.
"Berliners can feel with you and understand how the people of Spain are feeling. Fighting terrorism is something that doesn't just affect one country. We too have our experience of that."
Juan Carlos and Queen Sofia toured the Reichstag with British architect Sir Norman Foster, who is renovating the building ahead of parliament's move from Bonn in 1999.
The king also walked through the Brandenburg Gate, the famous Berlin landmark that was closed off to the public during the Cold War because the Berlin Wall ran next to it.
The king and queen are also scheduled to visit Bonn, Frankfurt and Dresden during their four-day stay in Germany.
